Being a member of a minority is hard. No matter how much acceptance a person gets from their family or social circle, they still identify as part of that minority. They have grown up with the sure and complete knowledge that they have something to be ashamed of because of the way society treats them. Accepting one's identity and coming out also means confronting the vestiges of a prejudiced value system. Relinquishing the thoughts that they are not equal is a challenge. This has been a lifetime of acquired value judgments and will not go away in a day, but can be challenged and confronted with affirmations and perseverance.

Remember that being part of this minority is special, amazing, and incredible. Individuals in this group experience love that they describe as deeper, more real, and much more intense than those outside the group. They embody out-of-the-box thinking and tend to be the most creative in both problem-solving and the arts. Being part of this minority is synonymous with success in many cases, and they often are leaders, inspirational figures, and catalysts for change. A spiritual leader once told me that a higher power created individuals in this group to show humanity that love would overcome any obstacle.

Being accepted by the people close to them is a basic requirement for survival. Individuals in this minority, who are often rejected when their families realize their identity, experience a unique rite of passage that is taken for granted universally—the acceptance and support of family. This alone doesn't end their minority status or achieve success. Every racial minority has this as a given, yet they all possess the awareness that the rest of the world will treat them harshly at times.

People in this minority yearn for equality and enfranchisement by the majority, just as every minority does. As long as it is an advantage to be part of the majority, it will continue. With recent legal advancements in their rights, it is a hopeful time for progress, but there are fears that some of these rights will be rolled back if certain political groups come to power.

My son (22 years old) has rather severe Asperger's Syndrome (AS), and my husband's nephew (21 years old) also has rather severe AS as well.

Individuals with AS can develop some coping skills to manage the anxiety caused by the frustrations of living with certain disabilities. Their cognitive abilities are usually not in question; individuals with AS can be extremely intelligent, but their unique challenges in communication and navigating social situations are more difficult than what is experienced by others with mental health issues. Their lack of focus on peripheral details and inability to grasp social cues that others take for granted can be significant obstacles. A tendency for extreme literal interpretation of communication, difficulty understanding sarcasm and humor, and often a very different perception of the world around them are hallmarks of my understanding of AS.

In my son's case, self-care is a daily struggle. He doesn't realize when his words provoke anger or distrust, and he often doesn't think about anything outside of his immediate interests. Anxiety medication can help keep him calm and prevent agitation. Many individuals with AS also have attention deficit hyperactivity disorder (ADHD), which complicates their ability to understand, comprehend, carry out tasks, and succeed in the workplace. 

Early diagnoses lead to social groups, therapy sessions, and psychological treatments that help develop coping skills to reduce difficulties. However, once an individual with AS ages out of high school, it becomes challenging to find similar types of support and treatment that are available during their younger years. They can be painfully naive, as they do not fully grasp what is happening around them, and many individuals with AS may identify somewhere on the LGBT spectrum.

It is important to note that there is no medication that can improve AS. AS has been identified and characterized by a set of behaviors, but it is not linked to any specific harmful disorder. There is no "missing protein" or "brain chemistry" issue that can alleviate symptoms as seen in schizophrenia or other mental illnesses. AS is developmental in nature, and without the coping skills gained from social interactions and experiences growing up, there is no quick or easy solution.

That said, he is in notable company; many famous individuals, such as a well-known tech entrepreneur, a pioneering computer scientist, a renowned physicist, and a historic president, are rumored or confirmed to have had AS. It is more akin to a disability than a disease, comparable to blindness rather than schizophrenia. Therefore, the potential for success is limitless, depending on the individual.
